outputs.L2:
(CNN) — On Thursday in Washington, floodwater covered roads, farmland, towns and parks, forcing officials to close a busy 20-mile section of Interstate 5 between Seattle and Oregon and raising concern about the federal highway north of Seattle. In Pierce County, south of Seattle, rescue boats were deployed Wednesday.

“At the moment, there’s no way to move commerce between Portland, Oregon, and Seattle,” said Bob Calkins, spokesman for the Washington State Emergency Operations Center at Camp Murray near Tacoma. “That is the main route into Washington from Oregon.”

Near Chehalis, south of Seattle, flooding left portions of I-5 under 30 inches of water, leading state transportation officials to say the highway would remain closed at least until Monday. State and local roads were also inundated.

“The problem is that the only really useful alternate route is flooded too,” Calkins said.

Farther north, in Arlington, a levee breach pushed the Stillaguamish River to the edge of I-5. The interstate stayed open there, though transportation officials said some entrance and exit ramps had been shut.

The storms also led Amtrak to halt trains between Seattle and Portland until Saturday, with the railroad saying Thursday on its website that “no alternative transportation” would be provided.

Across Washington, several rivers had already reached their highest levels, but water-covered roads continued to pose dangers. Officials said the threat of landslides remained severe, causing every pass through the Cascades to be closed.

A National Weather Service meteorologist in Seattle said the storm system, which had brought 15 inches of rain beginning Monday, had ended. Calkins said the rain affected nearly the entire state, but the western side of Puget Sound saw the worst impacts.

As the Puyallup River rose and endangered the city of Puyallup, Loretta Cutter responded quickly. Cutter, who manages a group home and has lived in the area for years, helped move 47 residents of Valley Community Inn — a home for people with mental and developmental disabilities — to a shelter at a nearby church. She also made certain that her husband and grandson evacuated their single-story rambler and reached safety.

“You never think you’re going to be in this kind of situation; you think it happens to other people,” she said from the shelter at Sunrise Baptist Church in Puyallup, a few miles east of Tacoma. “It was very traumatic for all of us.”

Cutter was among 40,000 residents in western Washington, spread across at least 19 communities, who were urged by officials on Thursday to evacuate because of severe flooding along rivers and streams. Calkins said only 260 people used the 39 public shelters Wednesday night. Authorities also opened seven shelters for livestock and two for pets.

By Thursday, the heavy rains of the previous several days had eased into drizzle, a familiar pattern in western Washington, even though the region usually receives less annual rainfall than Miami.

“Here, it seems to drizzle every day,” Calkins said. “In Miami, when it rains, it really pours.”

He said the flooding was made worse by warmer weather that melted as much as 7 feet of snow that had fallen around Puget Sound.

Health officials issued some boil-water advisories, but Calkins said his greater concern was what residents could encounter when returning home.

“The bigger problem is that people may have to walk through floodwater contaminated with sewage as they go back to their houses,” he said.

## Heavy rain and melting snow push Washington rivers over their banks, closing I-5 and forcing evacuations

**SEATTLE —** Days of heavy rain combined with rapid snowmelt sent rivers spilling over their banks across western Washington on Thursday, closing major transportation routes, suspending rail service and forcing thousands of residents to leave flood-prone areas as officials warned of contaminated water, sewage overflows and other public health risks.

The flooding hit hardest in communities along swollen rivers in western Washington, where saturated ground, runoff from the Cascades and continuing rainfall overwhelmed creeks, drainage systems and levees. Emergency managers said the situation remained dangerous even in places where rain had begun to ease, because many rivers were still rising or slow to recede.

### I-5 closures disrupt travel

The flooding forced the closure of sections of **Interstate 5**, the state’s main north-south artery, after water covered lanes in low-lying areas. The shutdown stranded drivers, disrupted freight movement and created long detours across the region.

Transportation officials urged residents not to attempt to drive through flooded roads, warning that even shallow-looking water can sweep vehicles away or conceal washed-out pavement.

“Turn around, don’t drown” advisories were repeated by local agencies as crews placed barricades and assessed damage to highways, bridges and rural roads.

### Amtrak suspends service

Rail travel was also disrupted. **Amtrak suspended service in affected corridors**, citing high water, debris, track conditions and safety concerns. Passengers were advised to check service alerts before heading to stations, as cancellations and delays were expected to continue until inspections could confirm that tracks and rail infrastructure were safe.

The suspension added to travel problems already caused by closed highways and flooded local roads, particularly for people trying to move between Seattle, Portland and communities in southwest Washington.

### Thousands evacuate as rivers overflow

Emergency officials in several counties ordered or recommended evacuations for low-lying neighborhoods, mobile home parks and areas near rivers and creeks. State and local agencies reported **thousands of people affected by evacuation orders or advisories**, with shelters opened for residents unable to stay with family or friends.

Rescue crews used high-water vehicles and boats in some areas to reach people cut off by rising water. Officials said most evacuations were precautionary, but they emphasized that conditions could change quickly as rivers crested.

Residents were urged to bring medications, important documents, pets, phone chargers and essential supplies if they left home. Authorities also asked people not to return until floodwaters receded and roads were declared safe.

### Public health concerns grow

Health officials warned that floodwater can contain **sewage, chemicals, fuel, animal waste and sharp debris**, making direct contact dangerous. Residents were advised to avoid wading through floodwater unless absolutely necessary and to wash thoroughly afterward.

Officials also raised concerns about:

- **Contaminated wells and drinking water**
- **Sewage system backups**
- **Mold growth in flooded homes**
- **Spoiled food after power outages**
- **Carbon monoxide poisoning from generators used indoors or too close to homes**
- **Hypothermia in cold flood conditions**

People with private wells were told not to drink tap water if floodwater had reached the wellhead until the water could be tested and disinfected. Residents cleaning flooded homes were urged to wear gloves, boots and masks, and to throw away food, medicine and porous household items that came into contact with floodwater.

### Forecast and emergency response

Meteorologists said the flooding was driven by a combination of persistent rainfall and warm temperatures that melted mountain snowpack, sending additional runoff into rivers already running high. While rainfall was expected to taper in some areas, officials cautioned that rivers can remain above flood stage long after skies clear.

State and county emergency operations centers remained active Thursday, coordinating with transportation crews, utility companies, law enforcement, fire departments and the National Guard where needed.

Officials said the full extent of the damage would not be known until water levels dropped enough for inspectors to examine roads, bridges, homes and businesses.

For now, emergency managers said the message was simple: stay away from flooded roads, heed evacuation orders and assume floodwater is unsafe.

# Washington state floods prompt rescues, evacuations and emergency shelters as rivers surge

**PIERCE COUNTY, Washington (CNN) —** Emergency crews in western Washington used rescue boats to reach residents stranded by fast-rising floodwaters as heavy rain pushed rivers over their banks, damaged roads and forced evacuations across several communities.

In Pierce County, rescue teams deployed boats into flooded neighborhoods where water had cut off access to homes and vehicles, officials said. First responders urged residents not to drive through standing water, warning that even shallow-looking floodwater can be strong enough to sweep away cars.

North of Seattle, officials reported a levee failure near Arlington that sent water rushing into low-lying areas and triggered urgent evacuation notices. Authorities said crews were assessing the breach and monitoring nearby river levels as conditions continued to change.

Emergency managers opened shelters for displaced residents, including locations equipped to help families with pets and livestock. Animal services and volunteer groups worked to coordinate temporary housing for dogs, cats and larger animals, while evacuees were encouraged to bring medications, identification, leashes, carriers and essential supplies.

For many residents, the evacuation came with little warning.

Loretta Cutter, who helps care for residents at a group home in one of the affected areas, said the water rose quickly enough that staff had to move fast to get everyone out safely. She described gathering medications, warm clothing and paperwork while helping residents — some of whom needed extra assistance — into vehicles bound for higher ground.

“You don’t think about yourself in that moment,” Cutter said. “You’re counting heads, making sure everybody has what they need, making sure nobody gets left behind.”

The evacuation, she said, was frightening but orderly, with neighbors and emergency workers stepping in to help.

Across the region, officials warned that flood hazards could persist even after the rain eases. Saturated soil can increase the risk of landslides, and swollen rivers may take hours or days to recede. Utility crews also cautioned residents to stay away from downed power lines and flooded electrical equipment.

Authorities urged anyone under an evacuation order to leave immediately and avoid returning until officials say it is safe. Residents seeking shelter or help with animals were advised to check county emergency management updates for the latest locations and transportation options.

“This is still an active situation,” emergency officials said. “If you are told to evacuate, do not wait.”
